query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, adherent alumina‐forming surface treatment on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxidation resistance at high temperatures by forming a continuous protective alumina barrier that retards oxygen diffusion, without detrimentally affecting its intrinsic room- and elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strengths between 163 and 530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, uniform alumina-based coating (e.g., via atomic layer deposition or electrospark deposition) onto the cast alloy surfaces.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at temperatures around 800 °C for durations up to 5 hours or longer, with strain rates in the range of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ during mechanical performance evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent alumina layer on the surface.
generation.mechanism: The alumina coating acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, preventing the rapid oxidation and subsequent pesting of the underlying alloy. Because the layer is thin and stable, it should not alter the bulk microstructure responsible for the alloy’s good ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with uncoated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the coated material will show significantly reduced oxidation rates (i.e., minimal pesting and scale spallation) during high-temperature air exposure while retaining similar room-temperature ductility and elevated-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Uncoated, cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr demonstrates inadequate oxygen resistance (e.g., pesting) under prolonged high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The coating must remain intact (i.e., not crack or spall) under the thermal and mechanical cycling typical of service conditions; its thickness should be optimized (likely in the sub-micron to few-micron range) so that it does not adversely affect the alloy’s mechanical performance.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness, deposition method, and long-term stability of the alumina layer on HfNbTaTiZr under cyclic thermal loads remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples. Apply the thin alumina-based coating to one group while leaving the other group uncoated. Expose both groups to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, evaluate surface oxidation (using SEM/EDS and XRD), measure weight gain, and perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar or higher weight gain, evidence of pesting) compared to uncoated controls, or if the mechanical performance (ductility at room temperature or yield strength at high temperature) is degraded beyond acceptable levels.

HfNbTaTiZr is a high-entropy alloy, and according to a calculated VEC value of 4.4, it has a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure. The alloy was developed by mechanical alloying from high-purity metallic powders in a Pulverisette 6 classic line planetary ball mill (Fritsch®, Idar-Oberstein, Germany) with a stainless steel vial and grinding media. Due to the powder reactivity, handling and alloying were performed under an argon atmosphere. To avoid the welding of the alloy to the vial and balls and to reduce the oxidation and contamination of powders, n-heptane was used as a control process agent (PCA). Milling parameters were selected after multiple trials to ensure that the powders were not overheating. A mixture of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr high-purity powders was milled for 60 h, and samples were taken at different time intervals to evaluate the alloying degree. After the alloying process, the particle size was reduced, and a good homogeneity was obtained. With further processing represented by sintering and deposition, the alloying degree was increased.
